utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We continue with our debate at 8.35. I have to say that I came at 8.15, meaning that I've been waiting for 20 minutes. So Mr. Registrar, when we agree to start at 8.30, we should start at 8.30 sharp and not at 8.35. Mr. Scott, you have 15 minutes and you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mufti Smajkic, you have heard just now we have only a very limited time. We only have about 15 minutes to finish this, so we are going to have to move fairly quickly, please. If I can have the usher please provide you with a packet of the final exhibits I would like to show to you. Sir, again, I'm not going to ask you for extensive discussion of these particular documents but if you can just tell us a bit about them and confirm them to us, that would be most helpful. If I can please direct your attention and the courtroom's attention first of all to Exhibit P 02563.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this a document that you wrote on about the 29th of May, 1993, addressed to UNPROFOR, ECMM, the Red Cross, the HVO and the bishop concerning various matters that you were -- concerns that you were raising with them about events in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is quite correct. And in addition, there is a letter here which was addressed to the Holy Father in the Vatican.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. I'll come to that document next. The -- among other things in the first document, P 02563, one of the items that you raise there is the destruction of the Balinovac mosque; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It actually lists four mosques which remained in the western part of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we don't have this document. I wonder whether it might be placed on the ELMO if it's a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We don't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Should have been in e-court. That's all of the documents, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can move, then, please, sir, to Exhibit -- the next exhibit I would like you to direct your attention to and the courtroom's attention to is P 02797. I'll ask the e-court to try to follow along, please, as quickly as possible. Mufti Smajkic, can you tell us what that letter is, Exhibit 2797?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document attests to our persistent efforts in addition to the Catholic authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Mr. Kuharic was the head then, it was our attempt to inform them firsthand with the -- about the unlimited extensive scope of devastation of facilities and buildings. So when this didn't prove to be fruitful, we actually got the idea that we should have such news reach His Excellency, the Holy Father, Pope Wojtila, and as at that time, the communications were down, were restricted, we had no direct contact, of course, and we used our connections with the staff of UNPROFOR in Medjugorje and we wrote this letter in order to inform the world public of the atrocities of the terrible things going on in Mostar. If you will allow me, I stated in this letter, because that same year, in January, I actually paid a visit to Mr. Wojtila together with the Bishop Peric, so I should like to inform the Trial Chamber that whatever initiative we took, however hard we tried to launch an initiative in order to improve the situation, and put an end to the sufferings which were happening to any -- as well as to any potential ones, that is why we took part in that particular initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And if I can direct your attention and the courtroom's attention, please, to Exhibit P 02800, is that a copy of the -- the letter that you sent to the Pope on the 16th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to Exhibit P 02852. And sir, is this a letter that you wrote to the -- excuse me, is this a letter that was written to you by Bishop Peric in response to some of your correspondence in which you had raised various concerns to him?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the correspondence that we had with the bishop.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. If I can direct your attention now to Exhibit P 02926, is this a letter that you sent to Bishop Peric on the 24th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, did you persist in a series of correspondence, communications with Bishop Peric and others again as continuing efforts to resolve the conflict in the Mostar region?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously we did persist, and whenever a possibility for communication presented itself, either by way of letters or by way of any messages to be sent orally or in other ways, we wanted to always tap on such a possibility and to establish contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very good. Sir the last questions that I would like to put to you is going back to some of the changes that took place in Mostar after the HVO takeover there. Did you -- were the names of streets changed at some point or at various points in 1993 -- 1992, 1993, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an official report from a Croatian newspaper, the Slobodna Dalmatia, "Free Dalmatia," but we also have a certificate from the local authorities of the municipality of Mostar which, as you can see, renamed the streets. They sent us the old names as well as the new names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you just a moment, please. You're referring now to -- you're looking ahead to, and for the courtroom, Exhibit P 08538. And you're saying that this was a publication, a published decision of the Mostar municipal council in which the names of various streets in Mostar were changed?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this document is proof of that, and it really happened the way I told. Not a single street remained bearing the name of some Muslim person of authority. Rather, all the names were changed to bear names of Croatian dignitaries, Croatian church dignitaries, and so on and so forth. Even still today, although the city has been united, we are still waiting a political struggle to change some names of the -- some streets, because they desecrated the dignity of the city. They have fascist names of fascist personages from the Second World War. Nevertheless we still have not managed to achieve a political consensus around that matter still. And this is indeed an insult because Mostar is on the World Heritage list. It is a disgrace for this city. There are about four names of streets, four streets with such names.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give the Judges, please, an example or two in the time remaining, of some of the names on this list that -- the renames or the new names given, excuse me, that is the names of people who you identified as fascist or Ustasha during the World War II period.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should like to draw your attention to the street under name 28, it used to be called the Aleksa Santica Street. It was renamed into Dr. Mile Budak Street. You can see it under number 28. In the second column you have the name Dr. Mile Budak. He was a minister, an official in the government of Ante Pavelic. As well, under number 33, the street of Jakov Baruha-Spanca, was renamed and bears a similar name, namely of people who did abominable things in the Second World War. The names are Vokic and Lorkovic. And there are others I can see very well here. I don't know whether there is a second page to this document. Francetic, for instance. Three or four names which especially grate on the nerves, irritate very deeply the citizens of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mufti Smajkic, thank you very much for your testimony. We have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should like to ask you a very brief question myself. I just familiarised myself with two letters; the one you sent to the bishop, and the bishop's reply. In the bishop's letter, you refer to a book that you had written, which is called "Instructions to the Muslim Combatant." It was allegedly published in 1993 in 50.000 copies. In that book, on page 26, it seems that you wrote that a military commander should adopt the decision on whether to release or exchange or liquidate some of the prisoners. Can you, as a clerical minister, as a religious person, explain to me how can such words be used, namely that a prisoner can be liquidated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honour Presiding Judge, I must correct this statement of yours because I -- it was not me who wrote that letter. That book was published, as indicated, in Zenica. It was written by the Zenica mufti and not by yours truly. It is true that it was published, that book, and it is true that it contains the statement which you have just now quoted. You have seen the resolution of the Muslims of Herzegovina in which we quoted the provisions from both the Koran and the Prophet Mohamed on the way how war is prosecuted and how one is to go about preserving human as well as other resources, economic resources included. You could have even noticed that it is prohibited to even destroy fruit and the fruit of fruit-bearing trees. So I can also tell you that in the bloodiest battle, which of decisive importance for the survival of the Muslims in the first stage of the operations of the Prophet Mohamed, the so-called battle of Bedro and, of course, the Prophet Mohamed has to be a paragon for all of us to emulate in our lives. That is the first example of a new conventional -- unconventional way of respect for human lives and prisoners. Actually, he punished the prisoners captured by the Muslim army by having each of the prisoners become literate. They have had actually to make ten illiterate Muslims - who were unable to read and write, in other words - literate. So this is an example that we can draw upon and we could actually point to to illustrate what -- how we feel prisoners should be treated. So the prisoners' duty, in order to be released, is to teach ten people to read and write. In the Islamic military strategy, there exists the theory which is quoted in the statement, the brochure that you quoted, which actually provides for the possibility of exchanging prisoners, the mutual exchange of prisoners. It is also possible to ransom prisoners, and as an ultimate possibility -- of course this is just a possibility and it is left to a discretionary decision, but, of course, when you have people who have committed massacres and very heinous crimes -- but anyway, it is possible that the military staff, the military court staff who are making such decisions, they may be able to mete out the death penalty in such circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I shall give the floor to the Defence to start the cross-examination in the sequence which you feel suits you best.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Defence for Mr. Stojic will begin. However, I should note for the record that we met yesterday, we believe that we need a combined amount of eight hours for cross-examination, we demand eight hours of cross-examination. And we are each prepared to do our bit of cross-examination and not have to forfeit it in order for others to benefit time-wise. So I've already informed the Prosecutor what we were -- of the time that we needed. I'm just making this record right now, but I think it's important. The Prosecutor indicated this is an important witness. Just on that last question, that would deserve a 15- or 20-minute response, especially when we go back and see what the gentleman testified with respect to this particular question that you raised, Mr. President, in the Tuta case, because I dare say it is very different. And this is why we need to take our time with this particular witness because we are going to find out that there is a great deal of confabulation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, it seems to me that we shall be having a problem early next week with a scheduled witness. Meaning that we could have Friday -- sorry, Monday or Tuesday free. All right. Then we agree? Sir, would you have a problem remaining here until Monday or perhaps no problem at all in that connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would have a very big problem, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we too, as judges, have formidable problems. Would it be possible for you to perhaps alter your schedule, perhaps postpone some of your meetings on Monday and indeed remain? Because if the Defence is asking for eight hours, they will have four hours today and four on Monday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a scheduled an very important official decision -- visit of a delegation from Kuwait on Saturday. So I was actually counting on leaving on Friday, tomorrow, at the latest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But could you go back on Friday and then come back on Monday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm afraid that would not be practicable.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I'm speaking on behalf of the Defence and the agreement reached by us. If there is no room on Monday, if the witness is unable to come for objective reasons, then we wish to postpone the entire cross-examination for a period in which the witness will be able to spend two consecutive days in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I will go a step further. If the witness cannot come for cross-examination even later, then we should exclude this part of the record, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that's a rather extreme position, Your Honour. Your Honour, the alternative position - suggestion - I think probably others in the courtroom may be thinking the same thing but I'll be the one, I guess, to say it: If Monday is a problem, is there any possibility that we could meet tomorrow instead? I know we normally don't meet on Fridays, but if we could meet tomorrow and then perhaps take Monday instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Or this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I already said that we have to finish at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour, then I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. There is another possibility, namely Defence can start their cross-examination today and then we can conclude on another day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, the witness came here in order to serve the justice, so the witness was here in Tuta and Stela and at that time he travelled twice. In the first occasion he stayed a week and then he was -- his testimony was rescheduled and then he testified next time. He is in the contact -- he has been in the contact with the Prosecution. So the witness was very well aware and experienced, actually, that scheduling his witnessing -- his testimony here is difficult, it is influenced by many elements, so it was not fair and correct if the witness scheduled his other obligations in Sarajevo on such a tight schedule, like Friday, immediately after the last day of his planned testimony, that is not fair. The witness should be ordered to stay here through the Monday and Tuesday. That is my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But is there any possibility for the Defence to commence with their cross-examination, to do the first portion today and to do the second portion another day? What are the problems there? Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I'm not going to say that there is a big problem, but there is a problem. We planned our cross-examination in such a way to give each team an opportunity to cover certain topics depending on the time allotted to us and so that the next team can continue with new topics. We believe that this is an exceptionally important witness, and we think that the impression of the cross-examination as a whole is completely different if it is split in two. So I suggest that it be postponed until such time when the witness can spend two entire days in the courtroom. But, of course, we will comply with any ruling you issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fact that the first portion of the cross-examination begins today and concludes it on another day is not a problem, in my view. If the witness comes and then there is a break of several days and then he continues, it is up to the Judges to assess his evidence. We will be doing that on the basis of documents and transcript, not on the basis of any subjective element, so I don't see any problems in beginning today and concluding on another day when the witness has a more relaxed schedule. The fact is that it could have been foreseen that the witness -- this witness will need to testify for a longer period of time, especially when this pertains to the individual responsibility of at least three persons. It is quite reasonable to expect that the Defence would need more time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The Judges have consulted each other, and I hereby rule that the cross-examination is to begin today and that it will be concluded on another day. Who is to begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I would like to propose something that we used in another case, in Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case, and that was the proposal of the Prosecution in that case, namely to invite the most important witnesses to come here at the beginning of the week so that we don't find ourselves in this situation when the week is running out and we have not completed our work with the witness. Perhaps it can be scheduled in such a way as to bring the most important witnesses at the beginning of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That was your remark, which is quite appropriate. When we are dealing with an important witness, such witness needs to come at the beginning of the week, not towards the end of the week. All right, but we now yield the floor to the first counsel who is to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have two requests before I begin. The first one is to have the Prosecutor tender into evidence all exhibits they intend to use, because I will be referring to some of them, so in order to avoid the situation where we have several numbers assigned to the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You are quite right. Mr. Scott, what documents do you want to introduce, which ones?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I didn't do that because I was being very sensitive about taking any of the Defence time so I figured we would try to do it at the end and that's the only reason I had not taken the time to do it immediately. We offer Exhibit -- the following exhibits: P 00180, P 00318, P -- we believe that P 00374 has already been admitted through a prior witness, but -- all right. The Registrar says yes, so ... We offer Exhibit P 00375, P 00477, P 00731, P 01160, P 01167, P 02244, P 02493, P 02563, P 02565, P 02586, P 02797, P 02800, P 02852, P 02926, P 08538, P 08939, P 09492, and P 09559, and also the In Court exhibit 00020, which was the marked Mostar map. And Your Honour, at the conclusion of dealing with exhibits, I do want to make one comment in terms of scheduling, please. I won't do it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, can you please assign the number. You have them on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. Let me just repeat those numbers, and for the record they will be tendered and admitted with today's date. The following exhibits are therefore assigned the following numbers: P 00180, P 00318, P 00375, P 00477, P 00731, P 116 -- sorry, P 01160, P 01167, P 02244, P 02493, P 02563, P 02565, P 02586, P 02797, P 02800, P 02852, P 02926, P 08538, P 08939, P 09492, P 09559. I do confirm that IC 00020 was tendered and admitted with yesterday's date. This completes the list, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Mundis, before giving you the floor for scheduling purposes, just an information from the Trial Chamber to both the Prosecution and the Defence. This has to do with Rule 115 bis. The Judges will be absent for several days after the 12th of July -- June. After the 15th of June, the Chamber will be in full composition then and it is then that the witness needs to come back to complete his examination. He needs to come back on the 22nd of June, because from that date on, all four judges will be present. As for the schedule, next week, on Tuesday, there will be a Plenary Session of judges. They will be discussing a potential amendment to the Rules of Procedure, and this has to do with the completion strategy. This session is scheduled to begin at 2.30, which means that we will have our morning session, which will end at 12.30, and then we will resume for the afternoon at 4 p.m. and we will work from 4 p.m. until 7 p.m. This is the schedule for next Tuesday, because all of the four judges need to attend the Plenary Session of judges in order to discuss the amendments to the rules of procedure. All right. Mr. Scott, as for the scheduling issue, I need to tell you that when I say 20, I mean 20, not 21. 20 hours is a normal period of time that is available to other judges in other Trial Chambers, and I think that this will take quite a while, in view of the number of the accused and the exhibits. We have, however, the obligation to stick to this time frame of 20 hours. Therefore, you have 20 hours available to you. And it is up to you to schedule the use of that time in such a way so as to avoid similar situations. Had this witness come on Monday, we would not be finding ourselves in this situation. You said initially that this witness will require four and a half hours. You are in charge of this case. If you are not planning the testimony of witnesses accordingly, then we will have significant problems. Therefore, do your best to ensure that the most important witnesses come at the beginning of the week, not towards the end of the week. I applied this rule, this principle, in the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura case. Let us try to apply it here as well. This is quite a special case, given the number of exhibits, and I must say that Defence also tenders certain important documents into evidence as well, and quite numerous ones sometimes too. So we will be dealing with very many exhibits, practically unprecedented here at this Tribunal. These remarks are addressed not only to the Prosecution but also to the Defence. There is a similar case in progress right now in Rwanda with six accused. This case commenced in 2001 and is still in progress now. Therefore, if we want to work efficiently, you have to bear in mind the 20 hours that you have available to you. Now we are going to give our position concerning the lodging of the appeal concerning the duration of the cross-examination. While we are waiting for the Appeals Chamber to rule on this appeal, we will continue with the old principle, namely to give the same amount of time to both parties, except when it comes to the individual responsibility of each of the accused individually, in which case such Defence teams will have the same amount of time as the Prosecution. Now, let us see about our schedule for next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I feel I must address a couple of points, general points. I believe and I submit to the Court with all respect that the Prosecution is moving as efficiently as possible. We took this witness, this last witness in shorter time than we had predicted. We have done that with various witnesses. We have pushed and gone as fast as we reasonably can. The Chamber has to keep in mind that we are trying to present the case, the evidence, to the Chamber. If the Chamber does not receive the evidence that it needs to determine the case at the end of the day, then it is the case as a whole and it is the work of Your Honours that is damaged. If we don't have time to present our case, and if we have to skip over evidence and we can't present it to you, then it is to the detriment of the case and ultimately to the detriment of Your Honours, the Judges, because you have less evidence on which to make your final determination. We have moved repeatedly quite efficiently. Again, we took this witness in less time than we had expected. We used less than four hours when I had said at least four hours or approximately four and a half, so I don't think, Your Honours, that we can be criticised for not moving the case efficiently. As to scheduling, Your Honours, I must say scheduling is a huge effort that I don't think anyone in the courtroom appreciates as much as we do because you don't have to deal with it. It's a huge effort to get witnesses here, a huge amount of work goes into that with the Victim Witness Section, with the various embassies, with the individual witness, with our office, with the Registry. It is a huge effort. Having a window -- a long window of time from the midday on Thursday until midday on Monday makes it especially complicated in scheduling the witnesses and keeping them over from one week to the next when a witness is required to essentially sit in The Hague for three and a half days. It makes it very difficult to schedule and have witnesses waiting for three and a half days in The Hague over an extended weekend. It makes it very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but Mr. Scott, I have to interrupt you. I also worked as a Prosecutor, so you don't need to tell us all this. When you call a witness to come and testify here, you will proof that witness before the testimony begins. If we are scheduled to work on Monday afternoon, then you have all the time prior to that to proof that witness. If the witness is scheduled to testify for two or three days, you will not schedule other witnesses for the same day. The next witness, then, needs to come on Wednesday, and then on Friday afternoon one of your colleagues will be preparing the witness for the next session. So it is your responsibility to schedule witnesses in such a way as to be compatible with your other tasks, and if we proceed in this way, then we will work efficiently. In addition to that, we have to bear in mind the funding necessary for the work of this Tribunal. Therefore, when you plan your witnesses, you must not disregard this issue. It is up to you to come up with a good plan. I understand that there will be witnesses who will cause a problem because unexpected things may arise, the witnesses may not be able to come, we fully understand that, but if there are witnesses regarding whom there are no problems, such as, for example, expert witness Donia, then these are doable issues. When you expect to have some problems, when problems arise, please bring that to our attention, we will discuss it and try to avoid it. Especially in order to avoid the situation we had last time, don't bring all of your witnesses at the same time. No. Bring them one after the other. Otherwise we will have the same problem we had previously. Please continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We don't bring all our witnesses at the same time. They do come in sequentially through the weeks and the days. What you said is true, that various people meet with and prepare the witnesses sequentially. Unfortunately, that has nothing to do with the schedule in the courtroom. Again, it makes it very, very difficult when timing cannot be predicted perfectly. It cannot be predicted perfectly. You make the best assessment you can and it just makes it very difficult in a situation as today, when we get to the end of the week and we have a large gap, and to expect the witness to stay in The Hague for an extra three and a half days is a hardship on the witness, Your Honour. We will try to avoid that as we can, but you cannot - I'll repeat - you cannot perfectly predict and time these things. We will try to do our best, as we have already, to schedule the witnesses in the most efficient way. I cannot say that -- it is not possible to always schedule - quote, unquote - the most important witnesses at the beginning of the week. It is difficult enough to schedule witnesses the way it is. We have to fit in witnesses when they can come, and we will do our best to keep that point in mind, but we cannot, cannot, commit that that will always be the case. Every witness that we call is important or we wouldn't be calling them at all. And especially the viva voce witnesses as opposed to the 92 bis witnesses that we will be submitting in the future. So, Your Honour, we'll do the very best we can, as we have. I don't know, I'm not able to speak with Mufti Smajkic at this point. I don't know what his schedule is, I don't know what his schedule is the week of the 22nd. I think it's only fair to consider the witness's schedule as well. I'd ask for permission at the break to speak with Mufti Smajkic about his scheduling possibilities over the weeks ahead. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. You cannot meet with this witness again because we are about to start cross-examination and any contact has to go through Victims and Witnesses Unit in order to schedule the next testimony. They will pass the information on to us, but you cannot contact this witness any longer, not at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Then again I say this in front of the witness so the witness will be advised that, please -- that he please communicate his schedule and needs to the Victim and Witnesses Section. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I think that I might have a solution to help us in the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you have a solution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I proposed last week and I will propose again here in court that if we could meet with the Prosecution in advance, go over their witnesses with them, so then we can tell them what we believe our projection of time is, they can also tell us what evidence they intend to proffer at the time. It allows us then to give them our input as to how much time they need, then they can work around that schedule. I fully understand Mr. Scott's problems with getting witnesses, but if they knew in advance a little bit what our needs are, and then it might solve of these issues. That's the proposal. So if you could direct us to meet, we are willing to meet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What Mr. Karnavas says makes sense. Normally the parties do meet in order to discuss, and the Chamber intervenes only when there are problems. What Mr. Karnavas just said reflects the good cooperation between the sides. If you tell to the Defence in advance what your scheduling plans are, and if the Defence can tell you how much time they will need, that will solve many problems. I'm trying to encourage that kind of a relationship between you. I think you need to communicate among yourselves, and we should stay outside of it, and only if there are no problems that you cannot resolve, then should we intervene. Please go ahead, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, only one moment. That is just to say this: I appreciate Mr. Karnavas's suggestion, I think it can be pursued, but I note this: All of that information, all this information, was provided to the Defence on the 14th of April. We gave an entire schedule up to the summer break, including the list of witnesses and the estimated time of direct examination. So at any time up until now, and we will be happy to receive it next week or as soon as possible, we could receive in writing from the Defence their estimated cross-examination times. All that information from the Prosecution that Mr. Karnavas has mentioned just now has been available since the 14th of April. So I invite them to -- the Defence to make a response indicating the estimated cross-examination time for each witness, and I suppose the Chamber then can give any further guidance because, again, Your Honour, we then have to make a schedule based on these things, and if the schedule changes from day to day, we can't have a witness -- we can't make those adjustments on a moment's notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But you see what Mr. Karnavas just said. Imagine that this witness -- the parties meet and you say to Mr. Karnavas, and you say to him, "I will take four hours." And they tell you, "Well, we need eight hours." So we have four hours and eight hours. Altogether that's 12 hours, which means a part of the week. So in that case, you schedule the witness for Monday, and then there are no problems. So if the witness comes on Monday, then we conclude everything that week, we take it to the end, and there are no problems. So you really need to discuss these issues between yourselves. I believe that another judge wants to have a -- give a remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to give you an observation. Mr. Scott, when you give your assessment of time that you plan to use for examination-in-chief, there are quite considerable differences between the estimates that you gave initially and then later. Therefore, the Defence -- or rather, I think that there are really good reasons for you to meet and flesh this out, discuss these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am happy to provide -- well, let me say again: Let me start by repeating, the general information -- I agree with Your Honour Judge Trechsel that this has -- this can be done. That information, the general information has been provided for a long time. Nothing has prevented the Defence up until now from providing that information. I invite them to do so. I invite them to sit down with the filings that we made the 14th of April - more than a month ago - and for each witness indicate the estimated time for cross-examination and provide that to us. At the same time, Judge Trechsel, I appreciate the fact that we will update our schedule, our estimates as well. We have done that. Again, please understand, we have decreased our estimates. It has been because of the considerable pressure the Chamber has put upon us to present the case within a 400 hour time frame. We are -- it's the Prosecution who has the burden of proof in this case. We have been asked to prove our case in a very, very limited amount of time. I don't know if it can be done or not. I don't know if it can be done. We are trying our best to do it. But the point is when we shorten our estimates, it's because of the considerable pressure that we are receiving from the Chamber, and when we said we can do a witness in six hours and then when we try our best to say it's going to be four and a half hours and in fact we do it in less than four hours, that's where we are. We are doing our very best to do that. You cannot do this -- I submit again, you cannot try these cases by stopwatch. You cannot do it. There is inevitable -- there are human factors involved, and you make estimates, you do the best you can to make an estimate, but -- and that's all you can do. I'm happy to meet with the Defence, I will meet with them this afternoon, if they wish to do so. They have the information. I ask them to provide time estimates for cross-examination which will assist -- hopefully assist everyone, including the Defence, the Prosecution, and the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is asking you to meet and to mutually thrash out all those problems, because the problem that we have today between the Prosecution and the Defence will be in a different direction in a year, from the Defence towards the Prosecution. So in order to solve that situation, you will have to talk to each other. Ms. Nozica, I believe that you will start the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After all this, and as I need to collate the numbers, the Prosecutor's numbers with our own numbers, if we could perhaps take a break before we proceed with the cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Now it is 9.35. We shall take a 20-minute break and we shall continue at 10 to 10.00. --- Break taken at 9.35 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica? Actually, Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Before she begins her cross-examination, may I just take a moment to clarify the Court's ruling on our request for certification for interlocutory appeal. On the record this morning, I think the translation may have gone perhaps a little wrong at that point between English and French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will spell it out. When I said that we would be issuing a certification for the appeal lodged by the entire Defence, this referred to the previous case in connection with our oral ruling of the 8th of May. It is actually the decision of the 8th of June which is the subject of this other certification. That is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did Your Honour say the 8th of June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 8th of May. Sorry, the 8th of May. So I shall repeat: On the 8th of May we issued our oral ruling on the question of the duration of cross-examination. After that, all the counsels addressed a request, asking certification to actually lodge an appeal from that oral ruling. We shall be issuing a certification for the lodging of appeals. Did you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you. Will you be giving a written decision, Judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a written one. You still haven't received it because it has to be entered into the file, registered, but I am telling you orally that you will be given a written decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Madam Nozica, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Smajkic. I am Senka Nozica. I shall be interrogating you on behalf of Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said in response to a question of the Prosecutor that in 1992, in April and May, the HVO assumed civilian power. Can we see document 00180 of the Prosecution, which is a decision of the Crisis Staff from the 29th of April, 1992. And you were interrogated by the Prosecutor about that document yesterday in relation to certain points in this decision associated with your statement, namely in which way the HVO assumed power in this period in April and May. I will point to some of the parts of this decision and also connect -- link that with some other documents subsequently. Okay, we have this decision in front of us. Can we zoom it in, please? So yesterday we were talking about this and that is incontrovertible, you stated that members of the Crisis Staff and members of political parties who participated in the government at that particular moment, that the Crisis Staff, namely, was actually established because the Serbs had left the government bodies, and here we have the names given of Crisis Staff members and it is obvious that we can identify them as persons who belong to some political parties and some were not identified. For instance, Mr. Jole Musa. Do you know whether he was a member of a political party?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Fikret Bajric, that's number 8.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: He was also a party representative?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Ilija Filipovic also, is that also so?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mehmed Behmen?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Josip Skutor, Borislav Puljic, Zijad Demirovic - we heard that name already - Izet Hadziosmanovic, we already heard about him, and we know that Mr. Gagro was the mayor of Mostar in that period; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So now we shall dwell on item 2 of this decision. Item 2 of this decision says the protection and defence of the city of Mostar against units referred to in Article 1 - and that refers to the Yugoslav People's Army - is hereby entrusted to the Croatian Defence Council, the municipal staff of Mostar, as well as to members of the Ministry of the Interior, the Mostar centre. So from this item of the decision, can we then take it that on the basis of this document, the defence of the city of Mostar was legally, legitimately entrusted to members of HVO and Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this paragraph, one might have a hint. This is an assumption of something that ought to happen, but however in practice, in reality, this is not the way it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Smajkic, I will give you other documents to illustrate how it unfolded subsequently in practice, but at this moment please focus on this decision, will you.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, in regard to the second portion, the second part, the end of this Article, "and the members of the Ministry of the Interior, the Mostar centre," in whatever way it was or when the HVO assumed this duty, it also presupposed some other requirements, as indicated in this document. Anyway, in whatever way it was that the HVO assumed the leading role in the defence of the city of Mostar, it was not allowed to members of the Ministry of the Interior, which was a joint institution, which included policemen who were both Muslims and Croats. Actually what it did was to expel all the Bosniaks from the MUP and establish a mono-ethnic MUP. So that this is what actually happened. They derogated from this provision, in fact, significantly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who expelled whom, in which way is something that we shall be discussing later. Please, I'm just pointing out for you some documents, and, of course, I am quite aware of the fact that I cannot change your convictions, they are the way they are and they are your assessments, but they do not only refer to this particular portion of the text. Let me now draw your attention to Article 3 of this decision, which states in paragraph 2 that the Muslims may establish their own units to be placed under the single command of the HVO, the municipal staff of Mostar. Are you aware of the Muslims having established their own armed formations which were to be placed under the united command of the HVO municipal staff in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim forces or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina were independent forces that took part together with the HVO in the defence of Mostar in the first stage of aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina, but there were quite a few Muslims who were members of the armed units of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So we agree that there were Muslims, quite a few of them in the units of the HVO, and that they were independent units of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of the units of army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I can see that you react when I say "Muslim forces." As far as I can remember, at least on one occasion yesterday you used that term. We'll see whether you use this term in an official capacity. I'm not insisting on this term, I'm just quoting the decision and following, to a certain extent, what you yourself said. Let's have a look at paragraph 4 now.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I disagree with your position. In order to be cooperative, I used the term "the Muslim forces," but that's not an adequate term. It's the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which still had members that weren't Muslims, and as a result, the term we should use is "the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina." There was a small group, however, that was part of the army and that called themselves the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please have a look at item 4 of this decision. It says that the national composition of the command staff of the HVO shall correspond to the national identity of active soldiers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You had certain comments with regard to this. Yesterday you said that the HVO took over the command and you said that there were no Muslims who were part of the command staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to another item of this decision. It's not a problem for me to read out the entire item, but the Prosecutor drew your attention only to item 8. I'll get to that. But let's have a look at item 7, the last paragraph under item 7. And if we have agreed that the Crisis Staff adopted this decision and that it was the only legitimate and legal body of executive authority in Mostar at the time, could we then agree that here it states that all documents for the movement of goods and people are to be issued by the HVO, the municipal Mostar staff. Is that what it says in this decision?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see the first part of item 7.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we just scroll up a bit? Yes, now we can see it. Sir, so it's correct to say that that is what this decision states?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Please, with regard to your comment according to which the HVO took over civilian and military authority in Mostar at that period of time, in that period of time -- we are talking about the period April-May, 1992, and we are talking about a period during which a decision was taken to act jointly against the JNA and other paramilitary formations, against the aggressor in the area. Tell me, at that time, were the Muslims in the ABiH adequately armed, adequately organised, in order to carry out this task in an appropriate manner? Were they prepared to carry out that task in such a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the end of the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean independently?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes. Or in any other way. At that point in time, were the Muslim people adequately armed and prepared to carry out this task on their own?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not on their own.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were they adequately armed?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's true to say that they weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll now show you the following document. Could it please be brought up on the screen. 2D 0007 is the number of the document. It is in B/C/S. We only have the B/C/S version. I have provided the interpreters with the document. I've already said it's been submitted for translation. That was done on the 21st of December, 2005. And as soon as we receive the translation, we will attach it to this document. You have it in front of you on the screen. You have a report compiled by the Cultural Circle of Muslims in Mostar, and that was part of the Muslim community. It's an information, it's a report on the situation and problems in Mostar and Herzegovina. And here it says it's a working version. Let's just scroll down a little so that we can see the date, so that we can see when this report was drafted. So it was in September, 1992. Do you remember this report? Do you remember having participated in the drafting of this report? Do you remember it being presented at a press conference? What can you tell us about this report? What do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of the title, I couldn't tell you much. I couldn't tell you anything. I can see that it's a report. I admit that there was a Muslim Cultural Circle within the Muslim community, within the Islamic community. We made various proposals that depended on the situation, we made various proposals to improve the situation. We drafted a lot of documents. Yourself have said that this is a working version. So I really don't know what it is exactly on the basis of the title.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could we have a look at page 2, please. You'll then be able to have a look at the table of contents and then I'll ask you whether you remember this report and whether you participated in its drafting. Could we see the entire page on the screen. Could we zoom out a little?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see it well enough. Now it's okay. The Cultural Circle functioned within the Islamic community. I can now recognise this material. I know that various people prepared various reports, and as a representative of the Islamic community, this was done in close cooperation with myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'll read something out from the introduction. It's on the next page, under the title, "Introduction." Could we please scroll down a little? A little more, just a little more. That's fine, we can stop there. Scroll up a bit again. A little further up. That's fine. Let's have a look at the introductory part, which refers to problems that Muslims of Herzegovina have mentioned with regard to the SDA. We are talking about September, 1992. You spoke at length about this and I think this introduction contains many things about which you spoke yesterday. You can see a part that's been underlined which says, "Because of these phenomena, the Muslim people in Mostar and in a large part of Herzegovina were unprepared for the war. They were not unified and they were unarmed. These weaknesses have been noticed by the regional board of Herzegovina, which, as far as we know, have requested for a meeting of the regional board to be convened but its president ignored its requests." Then it continues: "Before the war broke out, arms were obtained for Muslims and certain irregularities were observed at the time with regard to the distribution of weapons, in particular the distribution of weapons obtained for free, as assistance. In this respect, newspapers have published articles stating that weapons have been resold and this was accompanied by various manipulations. During such events, in which representatives of the parties were called out, they didn't even deny such claims. According to our information and from conversations with Muslims expelled from Eastern Herzegovina, we have discovered that this information from the articles is correct. And some weapons were sold for far higher amounts than the original price. And this has thus stained the party and the leadership in the pre-war period, and as a result, many of the honest citizens of Muslim nationality have distanced themselves from party leaders." And then it says that: "The president of the SDA regional board made it known via the media that units of the Territorial Defence of the town were being placed under the unified command of the Mostar HVO." We have already seen how this decision to place units under the HVO command -- under HVO command, was taken. You're familiar with these facts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and these facts are true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But since you've read this out, it's my duty to say the following, because Their Honours the Judges, the Trial Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm finding this difficult to follow. As part of the cross-examination, Defence counsel has to put questions to the witness but now you're reading out a report that lays the grounds for the question, and then ask him a question, but now he's answering a question before it's been put to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question was whether the witness was familiar with what's been described here and whether the description is correct.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't waiting for the question but I said that these allegations are correct. However, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I'd like to say that there are many things that you are not familiar with. That's why I wanted to say the following: Why did the Muslims not trust the leaders? Why did leaders of the regional board of the SDA have such a position? It says that the people no longer supported them or no longer trusted them. And that is correct. Why? Because they were selling the weapons that they had been provided with for free. There were many people who bought these things from the Presidency. Ismet Hadziosmanovic, they bought weapons from him and these weapons were probably received from the Croatian side. He sold them to people who had to fight, and I don't know what he did with the money. There were many others like him, but that was the main reason for which the people did not trust him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: My question related to the statement in this report that, as a result of all these phenomena that you have mentioned yourself, the Muslim people in Mostar and a large part of Herzegovina were unprepared for the war, they were not unified, and they weren't armed. That's what it says here. And I've put my question to you with regard to what you said about the HVO carrying out a putsch, taking over the command, et cetera. This is what you said yesterday, and I just wanted you to confirm whether these were your conclusions too, or rather, whether these were the conclusions of the institution that drafted this report within the framework of the Islamic community.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. I agree with everything that you have read out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the following document on the screen, 2D, Defence document 2D. And I hope the Registry won't hold this against me if there is a certain amount of overlapping between our documents and Prosecution documents, but this document was provided to the Prosecution and Chamber, and the number of the document is 2D 00018. It's a platform that we had a look at yesterday too. And the title of the document is, "The basis of the regulations of -- between the Muslims and the Croats of --" "The current political relations between the Croats and the Muslims." Can we scroll down a bit? Could you scroll up a little more, please? Could we see the middle part of the document? That's fine. You can stop there. Yesterday we said that you were one of the signatories of this document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And it was compiled on the 10th of July, 1992, and I'd like to draw your attention to item 1, paragraph 4, and I'll read out the following text: "We fully accept the fact that the Croatian people gave their major contribution in the fight against the common enemy, and also in providing care and assistance to the expelled population, as well as with the arming of the Muslims." Do you agree with this statement, the one that you signed in this document?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly agree but you will see later on that the documents were not implemented or complied with. If you look at the document as it is now, we can say so, that it's correct. Otherwise, I would not have put my signature underneath, had this statement not been true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that later on we will see that what was written here was not implemented, was not respected. You said this in the past tense. That is to say, something already happened and then you said to us that this is what was written and what happened. You said that this was in the past, that the Croats armed the Muslims, that they took care of refugees and gave a significant contribution in the defence of Mostar. Is that correct? Something has to be correct. Something has to be correct, Mr. Smajkic. It's either correct that the Croats did indeed do it and that you signed this, or they didn't do it and you signed it without giving it a thought. Just wait for a little bit before you answer so that the interpreters can finish interpreting my question.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that the Croatian policies in relation to that area were flexible ones and could be adjusted, could be changed from month to month. We did have cooperation with the HVO, relating to the liberation of the town of Mostar. That cannot be denied. In addition to that, we received assistance, the one that you mentioned, and therefore, it is beyond doubt that initially the people driven out of Mostar were assisted, were given care. However, simultaneously we had certain problems with finding temporary accommodation for these people, as they said, which means that they already had some plans on transporting these people to the areas that they said were predominantly populated by Muslims. So this was a sort of a silent war that was going on, and in this portion, we overemphasised the credit that should be given to Croats, but we did it in order to promote cooperation and liberation of the entire territory. We had to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who assumed what is something that this Trial Chamber will have to decide upon. All I'm asking you is to establish the facts at the time when they happened. This document, this moment, and this date are very important to us. It is very important for us to agree that the Croats armed the Muslims and helped them. Now, as concerns the refugees, although this is not my primary focus, let me ask you this: Did these refugees go from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some did, some --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Go to Zenica, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Some did, some didn't, but most didn't.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Humanitarian work is part of your work. How many people came to the area of Mostar at that time, both Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to give you any rough figures.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately how many thousands?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I wasn't focusing on that. We had some figures available to us but I'd rather not go into that now because I'm concerned that I wouldn't be quite accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I fully respect that. But I believed that since you touched upon the conduct of Croatian authorities, their attitude towards the refugees, that you took into account the ability of such a small town as Mostar to deal with such a huge influx of refugees, and we will get to their number later on. Now I would like to turn to the second part of this decision, which deals with the activities or conduct of the Mostar municipal staff. You said that this was a putsch. You said that the Croats mostly participated, but then you said today that the Muslims had no role in that government. Could we see document 2D 00024, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, when you give the number of the document, you actually gave us the number of the dossier, and you need to give us the first number, which is the number at the bottom of the document, so that we can locate this document. Otherwise, the other number is irrelevant to us. When you compile these dossiers, you need to mark them appropriately so we can find them. When you put your questions, I start looking for the document, and then when I find the document, you are already dealing with your next question. Therefore this is not helpful at all. If you want your questions and documents to be helpful, especially for me, then I kindly ask you to create a dossier, a file, that will enable me to find these documents quickly. Otherwise, it's pointless, because when you put a question related to a part of the document, I need to see the entire document, in case I need to put a question myself. Now, please continue because I have just managed to find document 24.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I thought that it was provided exactly in the order that you wished. And I would also like you to take into account that the examination-in-chief was concluded yesterday at 6 p.m. and that it was only in the evening that we started compiling the dossier. Since the hearing was concluded at 6, it was impossible for us to do it as efficiently as possible in order to make your work and our work easier. I will now call for the documents which are not in the e-court, and I will read out their number slowly so that the registrar can put them on the ELMO. I gave three or four documents to the registrar -- or rather, to the usher. Can we see, please, document 2D 00024. You do not have the translation for this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So this is a decision on appointment of the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar municipality, 25th -- 21st of May, 1992. Now, in relation to your remark stating that in the municipal authorities in Mostar there were only Croats, only Croats took part in it and that the Muslims were wholly marginalised. Now, in view of your remark, I would like for us to look at Article 1 and see who the members of this municipal board of the HVO were in Mostar, and let us go name by name, if you agree. Topic is the president. I will only assume, and I think that I'm doing that correctly, that most likely he's a Croat. Then we have Stojan Vrlic, who is vice-president. Once again I assume that he's a Croat. Mumin Isovic [phoen] is the director of the general administration department. Would you agree with me that he's a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His last name is Isic, not Isovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the man. I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And he's a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Under 4, we have Milenko Musa [phoen]. We can assume that he's a Croat. Under 5, we have Senad Kazazic [phoen]. He's the director of the department for economy. Would you agree with me that he's a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then we have Sejo Maslo [phoen], under 6, president of the department for social activities. Once again a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Miro Pandza [phoen], number 7, director of procurement department. I assume that you know the man. His name doesn't identify - at least, not for me - his national background. But we can be sure about number 8. That's Hamdija Jahic, director of housing and utility matters and revival, reconstruction. He's a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Then we have another name, Muslim name, under 12; Jasmin Jaganjac. He is director of defence department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: If we take a look at all of these names, members of the Mostar municipality board of the HVO, will we agree that your statement about Muslims not participating in significant roles in Mostar is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please come closer to microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Nozica, I'm not very adept at these things. You are a lawyer, a well-known lawyer in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is a routine matter for you. But you cannot mislead me. This document says what it says, and there is no question as to whether this is an authentic document or not. There are no dilemmas there. However, Your Honours, I kindly ask you to pay attention to my evidence. In Croatian policies, there was always hypocrisy. They appointed certain people to offices to show that the Muslims had representation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I apologise. A great number of your statements about hypocrisy and people acting in a double -- duplicitous manner, you gave us a lot of such opinions, but let us stick to our respective jobs. Your job is to testify, and my job is to identify documents and what they say. You gave all of these opinions yesterday and they were recorded duly. What I want to ask you now is: Is this true, now that you have touched upon hypocrisy, are you going to tell me that Jasmin Jaganjac was not a director of the defence department? Are you going to tell me that he was not a Muslim, and are we -- are you going to say to us that this was one of the most important offices and that there were many Muslims holding such important offices?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jasmin Jaganjac came upon instruction from Tudjman from Croatia, and he was supposed to soften that, in a way, and to attract, recruit, as many Muslims as possible to the HVO and not to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It wasn't my duty to collect documents. Had I known that such a document was going to be put to me, I would have brought you documents reflecting that Jasmin Jahic, later on the mayor of Mostar, Gospodin Sejo Maslo, currently ambassador to Denmark, Mr. Mumin Isic, and so on, these people resigned from their offices. I have their resignation letters. They did not stay for longer than a month or two in these organs. That's the full truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And that's how long the fighting took; would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please come closer to the microphone. We have great trouble hearing Madam Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said that they participated for two months only, which means that they stayed on until the Chetniks were expelled.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but they resigned.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We will get to those resignations. Let us take it slowly, please. I thought that you submitted to the Prosecution all of the documents, because you submitted a lot of relevant documents for this period and we thought that you were able to obtain all of the documents you needed. There is still some time. It's not too late. Now, after this, could we please see Defence document 25 following this one. I just need the first page, please. 2D 00025. It is in the dossier - in the file - immediately following this document. This is a decision on the establishment of administrative departments in the area of Mostar municipality.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We can conclude from this decision -- so we can conclude on the basis of this decision how many of such departments were actually set up. I have no intention of dwelling on this document for a long time but kindly look at page 2, page 3, and page 4. The only thing I should like to ask you in connection with this decision is this: Did you know at the time, on the 21st of May in 1992, what the structure of the executive branch of government was? Those were the civilian authorities, would you not agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Civilian authorities headed by Jadranko Topic. With Jadranko Topic at the helm. Will the Honourable Trial Chamber please pay attention to the heading of this document, which says, "The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and the Croatian Defence Council" without any reference whatever to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was just about to ask you in regard to document 24, 25, what explanation can you give us in respect of the fact that it is an official document and makes no reference to Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What is your explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is a question of paramount importance. It is a crucial question, because it strikes one visually immediately. We have already observed why it was that those people, the so-called ministers in this government, actually tendered in their resignations, because they actually observed these anti-state, anti-Bosnia and Herzegovina tendencies, a proclivity for the trend leading to the creation of an autonomous entity with all the attributes of a state, and that is Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Yesterday, when you were shown these documents, which indicated that they were documents, it was written on them that they were documents of Herceg-Bosna, there were others shown by the Prosecution which said Bosnia and Herzegovina clearly, and then under it, Herceg-Bosna. Did you have occasion to see such documents yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And otherwise?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Were such documents customary for the entire area?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to revert to this subject. If Muslim representatives left such a body that did not recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as its own state, and, of course, life had to go on, they did insert by way of duplicity, actually, to insert that into the titles, but the actual basic policy vis-a-vis the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not change.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You are saying our people left that government because of those reasons. Why, when, was it when the Serbo-Chetnik armada was expelled from Mostar, tell me, at this time when documents with these headings appeared, were Bosniaks participants in such organs?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We shall proceed. We shall see how correct that is. Can we have a document 2D 00026 placed on the ELMO. We shall have a translation submitted subsequently, but I would read the introduction. This is the 30th of April, 1992, which is to say in the thick of fighting, the fighting is in full swing, actually, against the Serbian aggressor forces, and this is an excerpt from the minutes of a meeting of unit commanders of the municipal staff of Mostar, of the HVO, held on the 29th of April, 1992, at 0930 hours. Attending the meeting were a large number of persons, and I shall just read out for your benefit the commanders that were Muslims, as far as I know, and you shall just confirm this for me, if you would be so kind. Suad Cupina, Semsudin Hasic, Arif Pasalic, Mufid Kajtaz, Adem Zulovic. Am I right, Mr. Smajkic, that these people are Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that these were unit commanders of the municipal staff of Mostar on the 30th of April, 1992? Do you have an objection in terms that some of these people were not unit commanders in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not read this document, but I do know these persons. They were members of the army. Some were with the HVO, but they represented the command, they constituted the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I have to repeat this for you. This is a meeting of unit commanders of the municipal staff of the HVO in Mostar. We have read what the municipal staff is. I just want you to tell me whether these people participated at that meeting as unit commanders at the time the minutes of meeting were drawn up.

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the date, I can tell, because I know when the activities to liberate the city of Mostar were launched, all the forces were rallied, the Muslim and the Croat forces, and all the units that were preparing an offensive strike to expel the other forces and liberate the city from the JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In other words, the people attending, the persons attending this meeting, as the Presiding Judge has also observed, feature in documents which bear the title, "Croatian Defence Council," but we'll deal with that later. The fact is that these people accepted to do this job together under that coat of arms, under that particular emblem?

utterances.speaker: SEID SMAJKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had to swallow something. They had to put up with something for the greater interests' sake, for the liberation of the city's sake, and of course expected that the situation would improve and that they would indeed have a united armed force.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the speakers please not overlap.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, you are here to answer the questions of the lawyer. You do not do that but you start pleading after every question. That makes the Defence lose a lot of time, and I would ask you, please, to stick to your role. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I will refrain henceforth but will Madam Nozica then ask me such questions that I don't really feel the need to give additional comments.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You cannot expect of me to put to you the same kind of question as the Prosecution did. That is not my role. I shall now ask for document 2D 00028 to be put on the ELMO.
